# Natural (human) rights (`natural_rights`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/ideas.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Scientific method & philosophical ideas (`ideas`)
- Deps: helped by human_equality_dignity, rule_of_law
- Core idea: Each person has certain claims simply by being human (to life, to liberty of person, to the fruits of their labour, to a hearing before punishment) which no ruler granted and none may take away, and governments exist to protect them. They are not facts of nature like gravity; they are a moral and legal standard against which laws are judged, and their force comes from being written down and enforceable against the ruler in court. The persuasive bridge in older worlds is natural law, which Stoics, jurists and theologians already accept: if a higher law binds the king, then subjects have something they may demand, not merely hope for.
- Pitfalls:
  - Treating natural law (duties under a higher order) and natural rights (claims of individuals) as the same thing
  - Calling Magna Carta (1215) a charter of universal rights; it secured privileges for barons and 'free men'
  - Asserting rights as self-evident to people whose moral language is duty, honour and status; translate into what the ruler may not do
  - Declaring that subjects may resist a ruler who violates rights is the theory of rebellion and is treated as treason
  - Listing modern rights (privacy, holidays, internet) as if all were equally basic
- History: greece: c. 441 BC – Sophocles' Antigone appeals to unwritten laws above the king's decree; 3rd c. BC Stoic natural law; rome: c. 51 BC – Cicero: true law is right reason in agreement with nature; jurists develop the 'law of nations'; china: c. 300 BC – Mencius: the people matter most, the ruler least, and a tyrant may be removed; a doctrine of rulers' duties, not individual rights; india: 3rd c. BC – Ashoka's edicts urge humane treatment of prisoners and subjects as royal duty (dharma), not as rights; islamic: c. 1100 – al-Ghazali: the law exists to protect religion, life, intellect, lineage and property; europe: 12th–14th c. canon lawyers and Ockham speak of subjective rights; 1539 Vitoria: the American Indians have true ownership and rule; 1625 Grotius; 1689 Locke; 1789 Declaration of the Rights of Man; c. 1796 Bentham's rejoinder, 'nonsense upon stilts'; americas: 1776 – Virginia Declaration of Rights and Declaration of Independence; 1791 Bill of Rights
- Read:
  - John Locke, Two Treatises of Government (1689)
  - Brian Tierney, The Idea of Natural Rights: Studies on Natural Rights, Natural Law and Church Law 1150–1625 (1997)
  - Lynn Hunt, Inventing Human Rights: A History (2007)
